newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Vranitzky named as guerrilla bomb target.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Vranitzky named as guerrilla bomb target.

text.p: Chancellor Franz Vranitzky was named on Tuesday as the target of a guerrilla threat to blow up prominent people in Austria and abroad.

An interior ministry spokesman said a group calling itself the Bajuvarian Liberation Army had written to current affairs magazine Profil warning that it planned to target eight well-known figures in a renewed bombing offensive.
The alert came in the midst of campaigning for European parliamentary elections and a Vienna state poll on October 13.
Officials had said the eight people on the target list lived both in Austria and outside the country but declined to reveal their names or the countries involved.
But Austrian radio later quoted the interior ministry as saying the Social Democrat chancellor, one of Europe's longest-serving heads of government, was among those threatened.
"Chancellor Vranitzky is one of the names that appears in the latest written threat sent by the Bajuvarian Liberation Army," the ministry was quoted as saying.

Police chiefs confirmed the note was authentic, because it bore the same hallmarks as messages attached by the group to letter bombs that have either exploded or been intercepted by police since the campaign began in December 1993.
"The government is taking this warning very seriously and supports the interior ministry in any action it needs to take," said Vranitzky, Austrian chancellor since 1986.
In a worrying development, the warning sent to Profil mentioned for the first time only of bombs.
"The fact that this message makes no specific reference to letter bombs, means that other attacks cannot be ruled out," Interior Minister Caspar Einem said in a statement.

Police suspect neo-Nazis are behind the campaign. Government sources have indicated that the Bajuvarian Liberation Army may consist of a group of middle-aged fanatics. They are believed to be obsessed with reuniting German-speaking peoples in Bavaria, the Alps and the Danube River -- a distinct region which existed between the sixth and 12th centuries.
The group has claimed responsibility for more than 20 letter bombs directed against foreigners and figures linked to immigrant or refugee issues since 1993.
Eleven people have been injured in the attacks.

In possibly connected incidents, four gypsy men died last year when a booby-trapped bomb exploded as they tried to remove a racist sign. And a police officer was maimed in 1994 when a pipe bomb went off outside a Slovenian language school.

Despite questioning around 50,000 people and poring over 400,000 pages of related reports, police remain baffled by the bombings, drawing widespread public criticism of the state's security apparatus.
The only arrests have been of two young neo-Nazis who were acquitted in December 1995. No one has been charged with the murders of the four gypsies.
